balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For easyJet plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For easyJet plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

loadFactor.title: Load factor
loadFactor.content:
Load factor is seats sold as a percentage of seats flown (RPK / ASK) -- the single number that tells you how full the planes are.

For easyJet plc: easyJet runs in the high-80s/low-90s most years; each extra point of load factor drops almost straight to operating profit because the flight cost is already sunk.

What to watch:

  • Load factor falling while capacity (ASK) keeps growing -- a sign capacity is outrunning demand
  • The COVID-era collapse (FY2020-22) and the shape of the recovery
  • Winter vs summer seasonality in the interim rows

passengersSeats.title: Passengers carried vs seats flown
passengersSeats.content:
Seats flown is total capacity offered; passengers carried is seats actually sold. The gap between the two bars is unsold capacity (1 - load factor).

For easyJet plc: both series move together with fleet growth and route additions -- the question is whether passengers are keeping pace with seats, or falling behind.

What to watch:

  • Passengers growing slower than seats (capacity discipline deteriorating)
  • Post-pandemic recovery back above the FY2019 peak (96.1m passengers)

costPerSeat.title: Headline cost per seat
costPerSeat.content:
Headline cost per seat is total operating cost divided by seats flown -- the airline industry's standard unit-cost metric, comparable across carriers regardless of route length mix. Ex-fuel strips out the most volatile, least controllable input.

For easyJet plc: management guides the market on cost per seat ex-fuel every result; it is the metric the low-cost model is built to keep flat or falling, while the all-in figure swings with jet fuel prices.

What to watch:

  • Cost per seat ex-fuel rising faster than inflation (cost discipline slipping)
  • The widening or narrowing gap between the two lines (fuel price moves)

askRpk.title: Capacity (ASK) vs traffic (RPK)
askRpk.content:
ASK (available seat kilometres) is capacity: seats flown multiplied by distance flown. RPK (revenue passenger kilometres) is traffic: seats actually sold multiplied by distance. RPK / ASK is load factor.

For easyJet plc: ASK is management's capacity decision (fleet, frequency, route network); RPK is the market's response. FY-only because the DCF's growth path is built off the annual series.

What to watch:

  • RPK growing faster than ASK (load factor improving) versus the reverse
  • ASK cuts in downturns (FY2020-22) and the pace of capacity restoration

fleetSize.title: Fleet size
fleetSize.content:
Fleet size is the number of aircraft easyJet operates at period end -- the physical capacity constraint behind ASK and seats flown.

For easyJet plc: fleet growth is the slowest-moving lever management has; it is set years ahead via Airbus order books, so it is a better read on management's medium-term capacity intent than any single quarter's traffic numbers.

What to watch:

  • Fleet growth outpacing passenger growth (utilisation falling)
  • Deliveries deferred or accelerated versus the order book disclosed in the annual report

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For easyJet plc: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For easyJet plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For easyJet plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For easyJet plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For easyJet plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For easyJet plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For easyJet plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For easyJet plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
